rationale:
Evidence: Iteration 1 (score 574, best) used kp 4.0, base_speed 1.5, kd 0.8 and the wide 16 mm sensor array. Iteration 2 raised kp to 4.5 and cut base_speed to 1.4, and the score fell to 477. Oval completion dropped from 80% to 50% and s-bend from 65% to 55%, with steering_oscillation rising to 0.34 to 0.39. So the kp increase, not the speed drop, is the likely cause: higher kp overshoots the bends. Slalom still never finishes (0%, progress 0.39, max_error about 0.063, just above the 0.06 m off-track limit). The sensor widening in iteration 1 was the only change that clearly helped slalom progress (0.12 to 0.39). Body width cannot widen the off-track limit, since the 0.06 m floor binds.

Changes from iteration 1: (1) Revert kp to 4.0 and base_speed to 1.5, since the iteration 1 setting was the best observed. (2) Raise kd from 0.8 to 1.0 to damp the overshoot that makes slalom leave the line and to limit oscillation. (3) Lower mass from 0.8 to 0.6 kg. Yaw inertia scales with mass, so a lighter robot should respond faster to the sharp slalom bends. The oval (2.1 s) and s-bend (2.45 s) have time margin under the 3 s limit, so a small speed loss is acceptable. Sensors and line_loss are unchanged.

Expected result: the oval and s-bend recover toward iteration 1 completion rates (about 0.8 and 0.65), and slalom progress rises above 0.39 with fewer off-track exits. Hypotheses: (a) reverting kp removes the overshoot seen in iteration 2; (b) kd 1.0 keeps steering_oscillation at or below 0.35; (c) mass 0.6 reduces slalom max_error below 0.06. Measurements wanted next: per-track completion, max_error and line_loss_events on slalom, and steering_oscillation on all tracks, to confirm whether the mass or kd change drives any gain.
